bp: A sequential recommender is the part of a shopping, media, or content system that asks: after this user's earlier actions, what item should come next? The system does not know the user's mind. It sees a trail of interactions and a catalog of items, each described by metadata such as text attributes. The paper starts from a practical weakness in that setup: the item descriptions used by many recommenders are not rich enough. A product, video, or article is not only a bundle of attributes; it also has a natural audience. A running shoe for marathon beginners and a running shoe for competitive racers may share many words while pointing to different users. GenAIR treats that target audience as part of item identity. It uses a language model to infer an archetype, meaning a textual profile of the item's ideal audience, then adjusts that profile-derived representation with real interaction behavior so it can serve next-item prediction rather than just catalog description.
wh: The hard part is that recommendation needs two kinds of meaning to agree. Catalog meaning says what the item is: its name, attributes, category, and descriptive text. Behavioral meaning says who actually interacts with it and after what earlier actions. Those two views can separate. A language model can read metadata and produce a semantically rich description, but the resulting map of items may place things near each other because their words are alike, not because users treat them as interchangeable or sequentially related. Pure behavior has the opposite weakness: it reflects actual users, but it can be sparse, noisy, biased by exposure, and weak for items with little history. Existing approaches that statically encode fixed attributes miss the role of the target audience, so they understate why an item appeals to one user group rather than another. The central tension is therefore semantic richness versus behavioral faithfulness. GenAIR tries to keep the useful language-derived audience signal while forcing it to line up with empirical interaction patterns.
naive: A smart beginner would take each item's fixed metadata, feed it through a strong language model once, attach the resulting numerical description to the item, and pass those descriptions into an existing sequential recommender. That is attractive because the language model can understand product text better than a hand-built category list. But it fails in two specific ways. First, it treats the item as if its identity were fully contained in fixed attributes, ignoring the people for whom the item is most natural. Second, it assumes language similarity is the same as recommendation similarity. Two items can sound alike but serve different audience segments, and two items can sound different yet often appear in the same user's path. Static semantic encoding gives the recommender cleaner words, but not necessarily better next-action evidence.
ap: The paper's core move is to make an item representation audience-aware before it enters the sequential recommender. GenAIR first asks a language model to analyze item metadata and infer an archetype: a plain-text conceptual profile of the item's ideal target audience. This changes the question from only what is this item to who is this item for. The archetype is then converted into a compact numerical representation in one forward pass, so the item can still be handled by ordinary recommendation models. The second move is calibration against behavior. GenAIR adds a training objective that explicitly uses actual interaction signals to reshape the item map. In plain terms, it moves archetype-derived item descriptions so their neighborhoods better match how users behave. The method is presented as general: it can be plugged into many existing sequential recommendation models, improving their item inputs without requiring the whole recommender to be replaced.
mech: The mechanism begins with item metadata and user interaction histories. For each item, GenAIR gives the metadata to a language model and asks it to infer the item's archetype, a textual description of the kind of audience the item is conceptually meant for. That generated audience profile becomes an additional description of the item, not a recommendation by itself. Next, the system turns that text into an embedding, meaning a list of numbers used as the item's position in a learned comparison map. The abstract emphasizes that this extraction is done in a single forward pass, so the representation can be produced efficiently rather than through repeated generation. Those archetype-grounded item vectors are then supplied to a sequential recommendation model, whose job is to read a user's ordered history and score candidate next items. During training, GenAIR does not trust the language-derived map as final. It introduces a behavioral calibration objective, which means it defines a penalty for disagreement between the item map and real interaction evidence. When actual users repeatedly interact with certain items in related sequence contexts, the calibration pressure adjusts the map so those empirical relations are better reflected. The output is an item representation that carries three linked pieces of information: metadata, inferred target-audience profile, and observed behavior. Existing sequential recommenders can then use that representation to rank likely next interactions.
math: The main mathematical object is a representation space: each item is squeezed into a list of numbers so the recommender can compare items and histories quickly. This squeeze is useful because raw metadata and generated audience descriptions are text, while the recommender needs measurable objects it can score. But the squeeze is also dangerous because nearness in the map must mean the right kind of sameness. GenAIR's first mathematical idea is similarity: items with related target audiences should be placed near enough that evidence about one can help with the other. Its second idea is sequence modeling: a user's history is ordered, so the next item depends not only on what the user likes in general, but on the path that led to the present moment. Its third idea is optimization, meaning the system defines what counts as wrong and changes controllable settings to reduce that wrongness. The behavioral calibration objective is the key example. It says that a representation is wrong when its semantic structure fails to match empirical interaction patterns, then training adjusts the map accordingly. The important tradeoff is language meaning versus behavioral evidence. Language can fill in audience meaning that sparse clicks miss, while behavior corrects language-only similarities that do not predict what users actually do.
dots: This paper sits squarely inside the recommender-systems family, where many papers are trying to repair the comparison step before ranking candidates. It also connects to the sequence concept because the task is not general item matching; it is next-interaction prediction from an ordered history. The user trail matters because recent and earlier choices shape what should be scored highly now. GenAIR connects to the similarity concept through its item map: metadata and generated archetypes must become neighborhoods where closeness means useful recommendation evidence, not just similar wording. It also touches language-model work, but in a restrained role. The language model is not the final recommender; it is a generator of audience descriptions that are later grounded by behavior. That distinction matters across the conference. Many 2026 systems use language models to add semantic structure, then need ranking, calibration, retrieval, or graph-style evidence to stop that structure from floating away from observed user behavior.
ww: GenAIR should improve over static item encoding because it adds the missing middle layer between item text and user behavior: the intended or natural audience. Fixed attributes can say that an item is a phone case, a tutorial, or a jacket, but they may not say whether it is for beginners, bargain hunters, professionals, collectors, commuters, or trend-driven users. A generated archetype makes that audience assumption explicit enough for the recommender to use. The behavioral calibration then addresses the main danger of generation: a fluent audience profile may sound plausible while still failing to match real platform behavior. By pulling the representation structure toward actual interaction patterns, the method makes the item map more useful for next-item scoring. The intuitive reason is that recommendation depends on both why an item is describable and why people actually choose it. The language model supplies a richer hypothesis about audience identity; the calibration objective tests and reshapes that hypothesis against observed histories. Existing sequential models benefit because their downstream ranking can start from item descriptions that are less shallow and less detached from behavior.
po: The payoff is better item inputs for sequential recommendation without replacing the whole recommender stack. The abstract reports that GenAIR integrates with most existing models while maintaining high efficiency, and that experiments on three real-world datasets improve various sequential recommendation models compared with baseline approaches. In practical terms, the method buys a more behavior-aware semantic description of each item. A platform can use language-model understanding of metadata to infer who an item is for, but still train that inference against real interactions. The result is a recommender that can rank next-item candidates from a richer account of item identity than fixed attributes alone provide.
limits: The claims depend on several assumptions. Item metadata must contain enough evidence for a language model to infer a useful target-audience archetype. Actual interaction logs must be reliable enough to calibrate the generated representations; if clicks mostly reflect exposure bias, promotion, or accidental traffic, calibration can preserve those distortions. The abstract reports three real-world datasets, but it does not prove the same gains for every catalog, language, domain, or cold-start setting. It also does not specify how sensitive results are to the choice of language model, archetype prompt, or calibration strength. GenAIR makes item representations richer, but it cannot by itself prove that recommendations improve long-term user welfare, diversity, or fairness.
